**Where we are ahead:** a clean, allocation-bounded, fail-closed codec built on `bitcointx`, so a `tx`/`block` payload is the same type the sighash code uses; pure Zig, one sibling dependency (`bitcointx`); byte-exact against the wiki hex dumps and the genesis block; every decoder fuzzed with an anchored corpus. Among Zig options it is the only maintained one. **Where we are even:** the handshake and relay-negotiation surface a Core v28+ peer exchanges at connect — `version`/`verack`, `sendheaders`, `wtxidrelay`, `sendaddrv2`, `feefilter`, `sendcmpct`, `ping`/`pong` — plus `inv`/`getdata`/`notfound`, `getheaders`/`headers`, `getblocks`, `tx`, `block`, `mempool`, `addr`/`getaddr`. A header-sync tool or a tx/block relay/monitor tool can do its whole job with this module (compact blocks are optional: an un-negotiated peer falls back to `inv`/`headers` + `getdata`). **Where we are behind (→ Backlog, gaps a user will hit):** no `addrv2` decoder — legacy `addr` from Core omits Tor v3/I2P/CJDNS peers, and Tor is ~63% of reachable nodes (Bitnodes snapshot, March 2026, via search result — inferred), so a **crawler** sees roughly a third of the reachable network; and a caller who sends `sendaddrv2` (which this module offers) then gets `addrv2` it cannot decode. No BIP157 `getcfilters`/`cfilter`/`getcfheaders`/`cfheaders`/`getcfcheckpt`/`cfcheckpt` — with BIP37 bloom off by default in Core since v0.19 *(inferred)*, a **light client** that will not download full blocks has no protocol to use. Backlog-grade (not what a typical user hits): BIP152 `cmpctblock`/`getblocktxn`/`blocktxn`, BIP324 v2 transport (Core still accepts v1 *(inferred)*). Two of the three typical users named for this survey (light client, crawler, relay tool) hit a gap, hence `mvp`, not `core`.

## Design & invariants

Pure codec, no I/O, no allocation beyond what the caller's `Allocator` provides (except
`envelope.zig`'s magic-byte lookups and `block_header.zig`'s `blockHash`, which touch no
allocator at all — fixed-size stack buffers). Twelve files:

- `envelope.zig` — magic bytes for the four networks, the 24-byte header (magic + 12-byte
  NUL-padded command + little-endian length + double-SHA256 checksum), `decodeMessage`/
  `encodeMessage`. This is the untrusted-input boundary every other decoder in this module sits
  behind — see that file's module doc comment for the exact fail-closed check order (magic, then
  length-vs-ceiling, then length-vs-actual-remaining, then checksum).
- `message.zig` — a little-endian `Reader`/`Writer` (Bitcoin's wire format is little-endian
  throughout except `net_addr`'s `port` field, which is big-endian/"network byte order" per spec)
  plus CompactSize/`var_str` helpers built directly on `bitcointx.decodeCompactSize`/
  `encodeCompactSize` — Bitcoin's varint is one format shared by transactions, inventory lists, and
  address lists, and `bitcointx` already implements it byte-exact and fuzzed, so it is never
  redefined here.
- `net_addr.zig` — the `net_addr` peer-address structure, in both its no-timestamp (`version`
  message) and timestamp-prefixed (`addr` message, `TimedNetAddr`) forms, plus an IPv4-mapped-IPv6
  bridge (`ipv4()`/`fromIpv4`).
- `handshake.zig` — `version` + `verack`.
- `block_header.zig` — the 80-byte block header + `blockHash()` (double-SHA256 of the fixed
  80-byte serialization, matching `bitcointx.hash256.sha256d`'s use for `txid`/`wtxid`).
- `inventory.zig` — `inv_vect` (+ the shared `inv`/`getdata`/`notfound` payload shape), the shared
  `getblocks`/`getheaders` block-locator shape, and `headers`.
- `block.zig` — `tx`/`block`, reusing `bitcointx` directly (see "Reuse of `bitcointx`" below).
- `housekeeping.zig` — `ping`/`pong`, `addr`/`getaddr`, `reject`. `reject` (BIP61) is implemented but
  deprecated: Bitcoin Core deprecated it in v0.18.0, disabled it by default in v0.19 and removed it in
  v0.20.0 (github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin PR #15437) over the fingerprinting/bandwidth concerns BIP61
  itself documents, so no mainline peer sends it today. It stays because the wire format is simple and
  well specified and some non-Core implementations or very old peers may still emit it; a caller must
  not expect one back from a modern Core node nor build handshake logic that waits on it.
- `relay.zig` — the feature/relay-policy messages around the handshake: `sendheaders`, `wtxidrelay`,
  `sendaddrv2`, `mempool` (payload-less, checked by `expectEmpty`), `feefilter`, `sendcmpct`.
- `addrv2.zig` — BIP155 `addrv2`. Follows Bitcoin Core's deserializer (BIP155 table of network ids and lengths, 1000 entries,
  512-octet addresses): a known id with the wrong length, an over-long address or a big count is an error; an unknown id is
  kept; `Entry.usable()` is false for TorV2, unknown ids, CJDNS without the 0xFC prefix and IPv6 in the IPv4-mapped / 6to4 /
  Teredo / OnionCat / internal ranges, which Core skips without dropping the message.
- `compact_filters.zig` — the six BIP157 messages (fixed fields and 32-octet hash lists; trailing bytes are an error) and the
  `sha256d` chain helpers.
- `compact_block.zig` — BIP152 `cmpctblock`/`getblocktxn`/`blocktxn`; differential indexes (each difference and absolute index
  at most 65535, as Core), the 66666 element bound, prefilled transactions through `bitcointx`; `shortIdKey`/`shortId`
  (SipHash-2-4 over `SHA256(header || nonce)`, low 6 octets) checked against an independent SipHash (`tools/shortid_kat.py`).

Concurrency: `.reentrant` — every function is a pure transform over caller-owned values, no
shared/global state.

## Reuse of `bitcointx` — what was reused vs. what had to be written

The task this module answers explicitly asked: check what `bitcointx` exposes and depend on it;
say if its shape isn't reusable rather than duplicating the parser. What `bitcointx` exposes at its
root (`Transaction`/`OutPoint`/`TxIn`/`TxOut`/`Witness`, `deserialize`/`deserializePartial`/
`serialize`/`serializeLegacy`/`serializeSegwit`, `encodeCompactSize`/`decodeCompactSize`/
`compactSizeLen`, and `hash256.sha256d`) turned out to be reusable **twice over**, not just once:

1. **The `tx` message payload IS `bitcointx`'s wire format, unchanged.** A `tx` message's payload
   is exactly one transaction in `bitcointx`'s legacy-or-BIP144-segwit wire form — `root.zig`
   re-exports `bitcointx.deserialize`/`bitcointx.serialize` directly as `decodeTx`/`serializeTx`,
   with zero new parsing code.
2. **The `block` message's transaction list rides `bitcointx.deserializePartial` exactly as its own
   doc comment anticipates.** That function's doc comment reads: "so a caller can decode several
   transactions packed back-to-back, e.g. from a `getdata`/block payload" — `block.zig`'s
   `decodeBlock` is that caller, looping `deserializePartial` over the remaining bytes and
   advancing by each call's reported `consumed` count. This also means `decodeBlock` inherits
   `bitcointx`'s own hostile-input safety property for free: a hostile huge `txn_count` can never
   force a large allocation, because the loop only appends a `Transaction` after
   `deserializePartial` has already fully, successfully parsed one (see `block.zig`'s module doc
   comment for the full argument).
3. **CompactSize itself.** Rather than redefining Bitcoin's varint a second time, every count field
   in this module (`inv`'s entry count, `addr`'s entry count, a `var_str`'s length, `getheaders`'s
   locator-hash count, ...) goes through `message.zig`'s `Reader.compactSize`/`Writer.putCompactSize`,
   which are thin wrappers over `bitcointx.decodeCompactSize`/`encodeCompactSize` — one
   byte-exact, fuzzed CompactSize implementation for the whole repo, not two.

What genuinely had to be written new (not duplicating anything `bitcointx` had): the envelope
(magic/command/length/checksum — outside `bitcointx`'s scope entirely, it operates on an
already-extracted payload), `net_addr`, the `version`/`verack` handshake, `inv_vect`/inventory
lists, the block-locator shape, and the 80-byte block header (`bitcointx` never had a block-header
type — its scope was always transaction (de)serialization + sighash, never blocks).

## Threat model / out of scope

`envelope.zig`'s `decodeMessage` is this module's untrusted-input boundary (see its own module doc
comment for the exact three-check order). Every other decoder in this module assumes its input
already passed that gate, but is independently fuzzed and hostile-input-tested anyway (defense in
depth — a caller could hand a decoder raw bytes directly, bypassing the envelope, e.g. when
decoding a PSBT-embedded or otherwise out-of-band transaction via `decodeTx`).

**Documented protocol maximums are enforced where the spec states one, not invented where it
doesn't:**

- `inv`/`getdata`/`notfound` — capped at 50,000 entries (the wiki's own stated maximum:
  "maximum 50,000 entries, which is just over 1.8 megabytes").
- `addr` — capped at 1000 entries (the wiki's own stated maximum: "Number of address entries
  (max: 1000)").
- `getblocks`/`getheaders`'s locator-hash count and `headers`'s entry count have **no documented
  hard maximum** in the spec, so none is invented here (CONVENTIONS.md's "model after a proven
  implementation", not "add a plausible-looking limit"). They still get the same remaining-bytes
  fail-fast bound described next.

**Every count-prefixed list, regardless of whether it has a documented maximum, is additionally
checked against `remaining_bytes / min_item_size` before its parse loop runs** — a hostile huge
count with too few bytes behind it is rejected outright (`error.TooManyItems`) rather than trusted
into an allocation. This is defense-in-depth on top of the real safety net (mirroring
`bitcointx.tx`'s own documented pattern): every parse loop in this module only grows its
`ArrayList` one successfully-parsed item at a time, so even without this check a hostile count could
never by itself force a large allocation — the first out-of-bounds item read fails closed with
`error.Truncated` first. The two real bugs this exact shape produced elsewhere in this repo this
week (an out-of-bounds write and a 4-byte input demanding a 29 TB allocation, both from a
length/count read off the wire and trusted before the buffer was known to hold it) are exactly what
both layers of this defense target.

**`envelope.zig`'s `MAX_PAYLOAD_LENGTH`** (4,000,000 bytes) is Bitcoin Core's own
`MAX_PROTOCOL_MESSAGE_LENGTH` (`src/net.h`, github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin) — checked against the
header's declared `length` *before* that length is ever used to slice `bytes`, independent of (and
prior to) the ordinary truncation check against `bytes.len`.

### Connection-lifecycle concerns explicitly NOT this module's job

(See README.md's "Scope: a codec, not a node" for the summary; this is the auditor-level detail.)
Stream resynchronization after a bad magic/checksum, handshake sequencing (send `version`, wait for
the peer's `version` and `verack` before accepting anything else — the wiki: "No further
communication is possible until both peers have exchanged their version"), protocol-version
negotiation (choosing the lower of the two peers' advertised versions and gating optional fields
like `relay` on it), ban scoring / misbehavior tracking, and retry/reconnect policy are all
caller-owned. This module's `decodeMessage`/`decode*` functions are pure transforms: give them
bytes, get a typed value or a typed error, with no memory of any previous call.

## Verification

Run: `scripts/modtest btcp2p`. Tests sit beside the code in each `src/*.zig`.

- **Envelope** (`envelope.zig`): the Bitcoin wiki's own published `verack` hex dump and the envelope of the
  modern-(60002)-`version` dump (magic/command/length/checksum) byte-exact, both taken from
  en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Protocol_documentation rather than transcribed from memory, plus an in-house
  cross-check that `sha256d("")`'s first 4 bytes equal the wiki's published `verack` checksum; the
  check order, the printable-range edges of a command, a declared length of exactly
  `MAX_PAYLOAD_LENGTH`, encoder `PayloadTooLarge`, and `consumed` across two back-to-back frames.
- **`version`** (`handshake.zig`): the wiki's field-by-field breakdown of the same modern example
  (`version`/`services`/`timestamp`/both `net_addr` fields/`nonce`/`user_agent`/`start_height`)
  byte-exact, then re-serialized and compared with the original payload.
- **`net_addr`/`addr`** (`net_addr.zig`, `housekeeping.zig`): the wiki's "Hexdump example of Network
  address structure" and "Hexdump example of addr message" byte-exact.
- **`block_header`/`block`** (`block_header.zig`, `block.zig`): the real, published genesis-block raw bytes
  (en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Genesis_block) end to end (the 80-byte header, the CompactSize transaction count,
  the coinbase transaction via `bitcointx.deserializePartial`), re-serialized byte-exact, and the
  well-known genesis hash `000000000019d6689c085ae165831e934ff763ae46a2a6c172b3f1b60a8ce26f`
  reproduced from the decoded header.
- **`relay.zig`:** the four payload-less messages' complete 24-byte wire frames pinned in hex (their
  checksum `5df6e0e2` is the `verack` dump's); the `feefilter`/`sendcmpct` layouts, the `MAX_MONEY`
  range, Bitcoin-`bool` semantics and exact lengths are **in-house** vectors from the BIP133/BIP152
  field layouts, not external captures.
- **`inv`/`getdata`/`notfound`/`getblocks`/`getheaders`/`headers`/`reject`:** the wiki documents every
  field (and, for `reject`, the CCode table) but publishes no standalone hex dump for these; their
  tests are labeled **in-house** (hand-built from the documented field layout) alongside encode-decode
  **self round-trips**. Every hostile-input test in this group is likewise in-house.
- **Limits:** the `MAX_INV_ENTRIES` cap isolated from the remaining-bytes guard and at its edge, exactly
  `MAX_ADDR_ENTRIES` entries, a block with one `MIN_TX_LEN`-octet transaction, the user-agent cap.
- **Fuzz:** every decoder has a harness generic over its choice source, run by `std.testing.fuzz` and by
  the deterministic driver `BTCP2P_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]` (testkit's fuzz driver, shared plumbing
  in `src/fuzz_test.zig`). Harnesses: `btcp-envelope`, `btcp-relay`, `btcp-block`, `btcp-netaddr`,
  `btcp-header`, `btcp-varbytes`, `btcp-addr`, `btcp-reject`, `btcp-inv`, `btcp-locator`,
  `btcp-headers`, `btcp-version`. Inputs are corpus frames with a few damaged or truncated octets, with
  length/count-shaped bytes biased toward small values so the fail-fast bound code gets real traffic;
  reach tests run a fixed number of seeds in the ordinary test binary and fail unless every outcome
  label is hit. The two-layer defense (documented maximum where one exists, remaining-bytes bound
  always, incremental-growth loop as the actual safety net) is what these harnesses exercise.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module
  mutation run and the delta runs after it.

## What is deliberately not done

- **The BIP158 Golomb-coded filter itself** (decode, `matchAny`): `cfilter` carries the bytes opaque and `filterHash`/
  `filterHeader` chain them. A Golomb-Rice set decoder is a separate construction with its own published vectors
  (bitcoin/bips `bip-0158`), which this session could not fetch reliably; its home is its own module, not this codec.
- **A cap on `cfheaders`/`cfcheckpt` list lengths**: BIP157 states none for the reply (Core's `MAX_GETCFHEADERS` is a
  request-side limit, exported as a constant); the remaining-bytes bound applies.
- **BIP37 bloom filters** (`filterload`/`filteradd`/`filterclear`/`merkleblock`) — Bitcoin Core has served
  them only with `-peerbloomfilters` (off by default) since v0.19 *(inferred)*, and BIP157 replaces them
  for light clients. Listed so the absence is a decision, not an oversight.
- **`checkorder`/`submitorder`/`reply`** — "This message was used for IP Transactions. As IP
  transactions have been deprecated, it is no longer used" (wiki, verbatim, for all three). Dead since
  before this module's scope was drawn.
- **`alert`** — never, not merely not yet: Bitcoin Core's alert system was retired after a
  signature-forgery weakness was found in its trust model, and the signing key was deliberately burned.
  There is no key left to verify an alert against, so a codec for it has nothing meaningful to check.
- **Legacy pre-BIP31 `ping`** (zero-length payload, no `pong` reply at all) — predates every protocol
  version any peer negotiates today; trivially representable as an empty byte slice if ever needed, so
  it is not given its own type.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** published verack/version hex dumps used as byte-exact test vectors

## Backlog / deferred

None open.

## Roadmap

- **BIP324 v2 encrypted transport** — Core's default outbound transport; needs ElligatorSwift (secp256k1) + ChaCha20-Poly1305
  (`std` has the AEAD). Project size (weeks: a new module with its own handshake state machine, the ElligatorSwift
  encoding and a test-vector campaign); a separate `bip324` module is the likelier home. Backlog-grade while Core still
  accepts v1 *(inferred)*.
